name: nmap
one_line: network exploration tool and security / port scanner
plain: `nmap` asks a machine (or a whole network) 'which doors are open?'. It sends small probe packets and reports which ports answer, what service is behind each one, and sometimes the program version and operating system.

Think of a building with 65,535 numbered doors. nmap walks along and tries each handle. An open door (say 22) usually means a service such as SSH is listening; closed means the machine answered 'nothing here'; filtered means a firewall swallowed the probe.
Only scan machines you own or have written permission to test. In the CyberSci lab that means the targets you are given.

examples.title: Quick look at one target
examples.explain: Scans the 1000 most common TCP ports. Output lists PORT, STATE and SERVICE. This is the first command in most rooms.

examples.title: Every port, fast, then deep on what is open
examples.explain: Step 1: -p- means all 65,535 ports and --min-rate keeps it fast. Step 2: run default scripts (-sC) and version detection (-sV) only on the ports you found. Two passes are faster than one huge slow scan.

examples.title: Which hosts are up?  (ping sweep)
examples.explain: -sn means 'no port scan, just tell me who is alive'. The /24 means the 254 addresses 192.168.1.1 to .254.

examples.title: Skip the ping when a host hides
examples.explain: -Pn assumes the host is up. Windows machines and firewalls often ignore ping, so without it nmap may wrongly say 'host seems down'.

examples.title: Service versions and default scripts
examples.explain: -sV asks each open port to identify itself (e.g. OpenSSH 8.2). -sC runs the safe default NSE scripts: banner grabs, titles, anonymous FTP check, and so on.

examples.title: Aggressive bundle
examples.explain: -A = -sV + -sC + -O + --traceroute. Loud but handy in a lab. Do not use on targets that alert.

examples.title: UDP scan of the top ports
examples.explain: UDP is slow because silence can mean open or filtered. Scanning only the 20 most common UDP ports (DNS 53, SNMP 161, TFTP 69) keeps it quick. Needs root.

examples.title: Run one NSE script
examples.explain: Scripts live in /usr/share/nmap/scripts. Here two of them fetch the web page title and the response headers.

examples.title: Vulnerability scripts
examples.explain: A wildcard picks every script whose name starts with smb-vuln. Great for a quick check of old SMB bugs.

examples.title: Save every output format
examples.explain: Writes scan1.nmap (text), scan1.xml and scan1.gnmap in one go, so you can grep, import or share the result later.

examples.title: Targets from a file
examples.explain: -iL reads targets from a file, one per line. --open shows only open ports so the output stays short.

examples.title: Quiet-ish SYN scan on a range of ports
examples.explain: -sS is the default when you are root: it sends SYN and never completes the handshake, so it is faster and logs less. Without root nmap falls back to -sT, a full connect.

mistakes: Scanning only the top 1000 ports and missing a service on port 8080 or 31337: use -p- at least once.
Forgetting -Pn on Windows hosts, which then look 'down'.
UDP scans without limiting ports: they can take hours. Use --top-ports.
Running -sS without sudo: nmap quietly falls back to -sT.
Using -T5 on a real network: it drops packets and misses ports. Prefer -T4.
Not saving output: always use -oA so you can re-read results.
